text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with a negative externality, so I'm working out the payoffs: keeping a token privately gives me +1 but costs the other three players 0.3 each, a net social loss, while putting a token in the group account gives everyone 0.3 with no negative spillover, making it more efficient for collective welfare even though it's individually worse for me.

Since keeping tokens private always dominates individually, the Nash equilibrium is everyone contributes zero, yet the socially optimal outcome is everyone contributing everything, creating a classic free-rider dilemma where group-level cooperation beats individual defection in total payoff.

Given this, starting cooperative seems wisest—contribute fully to the group initially, watch how others respond, and adjust using something like a tit-for-tat strategy in later rounds.

Working through both interpretations, I find that under the "pays the depositor" reading, keeping tokens private nets me more individually (1 vs 0.3) even though society does better with group contributions (0.3 vs 0.1 net) — a classic social dilemma. Under the "pays every member" reading, group contributions are even more strongly favored socially, but individually I still get more from keeping tokens private since my own token gives me 1 directly versus only 0.3 back to myself if contributed.

Running the numbers with 20 tokens and 4 players: full cooperation yields each person 18+6=24 points, while full defection yields 18+2=20 points, confirming cooperation is better for everyone but each person's individual incentive still favors keeping tokens private.

Still, signaling cooperation has value for repeated interactions, so I'll pick a moderate middle-ground contribution, around 10, rather than fully defecting, and adjust based on how the group total comes back.

I'll start by contributing all 20 tokens to the group account in round one to signal cooperative intent, then adjust my strategy based on how others respond.
